title: No caste, no charms
hook: the code rejects caste, untouchability, charms, idols and lucky days

segments.voice: Yesterday, katha: a teacher holding one line of Gurbani up to the light and turning it. Your line was explained. What did someone explain to you, and did you listen to the end? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

A charm hung by the door to keep bad luck out. A wedding moved to a different month because the stars were wrong. A family that won't let a certain neighbor drink from their cups. Scenes like these turn up in many times and places, the Gurus' Punjab among them. People reach for them because life is uncertain and a charm feels like control, or because a ranking of people feels like order. The Sikh code takes these up, one after another, and sets them down. Today's word starts with the one about people.
screen: `A CHARM BY THE DOOR, A STAR CHART.` → `A CUP NOT SHARED.` → `THE CODE SETS THEM DOWN.`

segments.voice: In its section on a Sikh's personal life, the Rehat Maryada lists what a Sikh should not believe in. In paraphrase: caste, untouchability, magic charms and spells, omens, auspicious days and times, horoscopes, and the worship of idols. Notice that two very different things sit together in that list. Caste and untouchability are about people: who counts as higher, who counts as unclean. Charms, omens and lucky days are about fear: trying to steer life with a thread or a calendar. The code puts them side by side because, in Sikh teaching, both put something else where God should be. Caste first. Guru Nanak, in a hymn in Raag Asa on Ang three hundred forty-nine, says in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste, because in the world beyond there is no caste. That is the root. If the same light is in every person, a ladder of birth is a fiction, and a cup that can't be shared is a lie about the person holding it. That's why the langar is eaten sitting side by side in rows, and why the prashad we met two days ago is handed to everyone alike. Then the charms. In Sikh teaching, what happens comes within God's hukam, the divine order. A thread on the wrist can't bend it. A lucky Tuesday can't buy it. So a Sikh keeping the code doesn't wait for a lucky date to marry, travel or start a business; the day that works is the day. No caste, no charms. Every person carries the same light, and every day belongs to the same Giver.
screen: `THE CODE'S LIST OF REFUSALS.` · `CASTE: A LADDER OF BIRTH.` · `ONE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · `EVERY DAY WITHIN THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `NO LUCKY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one superstition. Settle, and breathe. Look through your own habits, gently, without judging them. A lucky shirt for big days. Knocking on wood. Not saying a hope out loud in case it jinxes it. A number you avoid. Pick one. Ask what it might be guarding against; sometimes it's a small fear. Then, for this sit, set it down. You don't have to throw anything away. Just let the day ahead be a day, no luckier or unluckier than any other, and rest in that. The bell holds the time.
No caste. The Sikh code rejects caste and untouchability, and with them charms, omens, idols and lucky days, because the same light is in everyone. Today's word.
Your line: no lucky days. Today, when you catch yourself reaching for the little superstition you named, skip it once, and see that the day carries on. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs not to believe in caste, untouchability, charms, omens, auspicious days, horoscopes or idol worship, so Sikhs who keep the code don't choose dates for weddings and other ceremonies by the stars.
